text: A model that only runs inside the notebook that trained it isn't deployed, it's a demo. Packaging turns a training artifact into something a serving system can load and run on its own, without ever touching the original training code again. Get this step wrong and everything downstream gets harder.

The format you serialize to decides who can serve the model later. Pickle is fast and native to scikit-learn, but it's Python-version-sensitive and risky to load if you don't trust the source. ONNX is framework-neutral, so a model trained in PyTorch can be served in Java or a browser. And native formats like SavedModel or TorchScript stay inside the training framework's own optimized runtime.

Here's a KServe InferenceService. storageUri points at the serialized artifact sitting in object storage, and modelFormat tells KServe which built-in server to launch to read it — you're not even building your own container in this path, KServe builds and runs it for you.

SageMaker splits packaging into three separate calls. create_model registers the artifact and the container image. create_endpoint_config defines the hardware and how traffic should be split. And create_endpoint actually stands the infrastructure up. Keeping those three apart is exactly what makes canary and blue-green rollouts possible later, because you can build a new config without touching the live endpoint.

So packaging is really three steps, not one. Serialize the trained weights to disk in a format that matches how far the model needs to travel. Containerize it so the exact runtime goes with it instead of depending on whatever's installed on the target machine. And then describe that package to your serving platform, whether that's an InferenceService, a SeldonDeployment, or a SageMaker model.
Packaging is what makes a model runnable by something other than you. Next, lesson twenty-two: how that packaged artifact moves through an automated CI/CD pipeline instead of a manual kubectl apply.
